title: Fostering orphan rabbit kits
subtitle: A foster doe is the only reliable option. Bottle feeding rabbit kits works occasionally; the odds are poor.
excerpt: Rabbit kits have the highest milk-fat requirement of any common domestic animal. A doe missing for even twelve hours after kindling puts newborns at risk. Fostering onto a lactating doe within the first 24 hours gives the best survival rate. Bottle feeding is a last resort with a high failure rate.
sourceNotes: British Rabbit Council kindling and neonatal care notes. Judith Bell, Rabbits (Crowood Animal Series, 2012), chapter on breeding and rearing. RSPCA rabbit neonatal care guidance. HRS (House Rabbit Society) articles on orphan kit care.

glossaryTerms.definition: A doe giving birth. Rabbits kindle in a nest box lined with pulled fur; the kits are born naked, blind, and entirely dependent on the doe's milk.
A newborn or juvenile rabbit, from birth until around eight weeks. At birth they weigh 30–50 g, are blind, and have no ability to thermoregulate.

content.text: A
doe
feeds her
kits
once a day, usually at night, for about three minutes. That single feeding transfers enough milk fat to sustain them for 24 hours. If the doe dies during
kindling
, rejects the litter, or fails to produce milk, the kits will die within 48 hours without intervention.
Finding a foster doe

Contact other rabbit keepers in your area immediately. A doe who has kindled within the past week is ideal, the kits being a similar age means the foster litter fits the nursing window. The foster doe's own litter does not need to be removed; rabbits readily accept additional kits if introduced correctly.

A doe with a litter older than three weeks is less suitable, she is beginning to wean her own kits and milk production is declining. Do not waste time on a doe who kindled more than 21 days ago unless there is no other option.
Introducing kits to a foster doe
Remove the foster doe from the nest box and place her in a separate space for 20-30 minutes.
Rub the orphan kits with some of the nesting material from the foster doe's box. This transfers her scent to them.
Tuck the orphans into the centre of the litter already in the nest, covering them with the existing fur and hay. They should not be sitting on top of the litter.
Return the doe to her hutch without fanfare. Do not watch, does are more likely to inspect and accept the litter if left alone.
Check after 24 hours that the orphans have fed, their bellies should be visibly rounded and warm.
Bottle feeding as a last resort

If no foster doe is available, bottle feeding can keep kits alive but the survival rate is low, particularly in the first two weeks. Rabbit milk has around 10-12% fat content. Kitten milk replacer (KMR) is the closest available substitute. Do not use cow's milk or human formula.
Warm KMR to body temperature. Feed with a 1 ml syringe, one small drop at a time. Kits must suckle; do not squeeze the syringe to force milk in, which causes aspiration.
Feed twice a day: 0.5 ml per kit at birth, increasing to 2-3 ml by week two, 4-6 ml by week three.

Stimulate urination and defecation after each feed by gently wiping the genital area with a damp warm cotton pad. The doe does this when she nurses; kits cannot eliminate on their own in the first three weeks.
Keep the kits in a nest box with a small heat pad set to low under half the box, so they can move off the heat if too warm. Target 32-35°C at the nest surface.
Begin offering small amounts of hay and pellets from around 18 days. Kits that survive to this point are usually past the critical window and mortality drops sharply.
